cards.title: Agent Architecture: what the page is
questions: what is the agent architecture page

how do her 29 AI agents share work
what is the shared queue memory and decision log system
is the agent architecture a personal project
cards.answer: It's the system design for the 29 AI agents I run across Skyrule and my other personal projects. They share one job queue, one memory, one decision log and an ownership map that tooling enforces, all on a single workstation with one GPU. The page covers who the agents are, how work moves, what stops them and what still needs me, plus Agent City, the 3D town I use to watch it. It's a personal project that runs daily, and the planned parts are marked as planned. I'm the designer and builder of the whole system.

cards.title: Why organize agents like a small company
questions: why did you organize the 29 agents like a small company

how are the 29 agents grouped
what is the product organization of agents
company analogy for multi-agent systems
cards.answer: The hard problems in multi-agent work are the same ones a company has: who owns what, who may decide, and how work passes between people without getting lost. So every agent has a written charter saying what it is for and, just as important, what it is not for and who owns that instead. There are three groups. The product organization is twelve departments of Skyrule. Four cross-cutting agents check, route and block across all of them. The rest serve my other personal projects and the machine itself. All 29 run on the same rails.

cards.title: What agents may and may not do
questions: what is the office of the founder agent allowed to do

what may the program management agent not decide

what does the voice writer agent do

cards.answer: Each lane pairs what an agent owns with what it may not do. The Office of the Founder drafts decision records for me but makes no ruling or ratification. Domain practice writes rule specs but doesn't decide what a rule means, and it doesn't write prose. Editorial verifies citations and prepares grading but gives no final grade. Brand and marketing drafts claims but publishes nothing. Legal and trust vetoes with reasons but gives no licensed opinion. The site keeper drafts changes on a branch and can't publish without my approval. The voice writer drafts public sentences and I approve each one.

cards.title: The Overseer: hourly health round
questions: what does the overseer agent do

does the overseer restart failed jobs
what counts as a stuck run for the overseer
after how many hours is a claude lane job stuck
overseer stuck thresholds 3 6 and 14 hours
can the overseer act or only check
how does the overseer ask each agent if its run worked
overseer up waiting watch down
cards.answer: Every hour the Overseer goes round every agent and the machine room. It looks for failed runs, stuck runs (over 3 hours on the Claude lane, 6 on cpu, 14 on the GPU lane), vanished processes, missed scheduled runs and offline runtimes. It also asks each agent, on a local model, whether its newest run did its job. Verdicts are up, waiting, watch or down. It only checks and never acts: nothing is queued, restarted or deleted. At 08:30 on Oct 19 it had checked 28 agents: 19 up, 5 waiting on me, 4 to watch, none down.

cards.title: Why one job queue
questions: why did you build one job queue for the agents

what is the cost of a single queue as critical infrastructure

why is the queue written in python and file based
who decides when a job starts
can agents start jobs directly

cards.answer: All unattended work goes through one job queue I wrote in Python. A job is a small JSON object: an id, a lane, a command or a prompt, and optional gates. Agents, the town and I can add jobs, but only the queue decides when they start. With several schedulers nobody can answer "why did this run now?"; with one, every launch is a single logged decision with its evidence. The cost is that the queue becomes critical infrastructure, so I kept it small, file-based and covered by its own tests.

cards.title: Queue lanes and concurrency limits
questions: what lanes does the agent job queue have

cards.answer: A lane is a statement about a shared resource: what would break, or cost too much, if too many of these ran at once. As of Oct 19 the cpu lane allows 4 (scripts, checks, merges, the Overseer, news desks). The vllm lane allows 1 because there is one GPU, and speed inside a run comes from batched requests to the server, not parallel jobs. The ollama lane allows 1 and no queued job has used it yet. The claude lane allows 22, raised from 16 on Oct 18 for a release push and due to return to 16; the code default is 6.

cards.title: The tick, lock file and idle GPU fix
questions: how often does the queue tick
what is the 15 minute tick
why does each finished job trigger a tick
what happened on oct 5 with the gpu idle
how does the lock file prevent duplicate launches
what happens to a lock older than five minutes
how do two ticks avoid launching the same job
windows task scheduler tick for the agent queue
what is a crashed tick
how does the queue run without a session open
cards.answer: Windows Task Scheduler runs a tick every 15 minutes with no session open. Each finished job also triggers a tick at once, because on Oct 5 the GPU sat idle between ticks and waiting for the next 15 minute mark wasted it. A lock file makes sure two ticks never launch the same job, and a lock older than five minutes is treated as a crashed tick and cleared.

cards.title: Gates, attempts and retries
questions: what gates can a queue job have

what happens if the wrapper vanished after a reboot
what is a not-before time on a job
how many jobs carried a priority
cards.answer: Of the 1,129 jobs added since Oct 2, 247 waited on other jobs, 61 had a not-before time, 120 had a start condition, 151 had a finish check and 373 carried a priority. The finish check decides "done" by evidence rather than by exit code. A job gets 3 attempts unless it says otherwise, and if the wrapper itself vanished, say after a reboot, the job goes back to the queue. Across 1,141 launches the queue made 65 automatic retries. As of Oct 19, 7 jobs ended failed and 49 were cancelled.

cards.title: The Claude launch budget and usage limits
questions: how do you budget claude usage for agents

cards.answer: The Claude lane spends my own usage, so it's opt-in per job: a job without an approval note never starts there. A weekly budget caps launches at 130 this week, set by me, so at least half my weekly usage stays free for my own work. When Claude reports a usage limit, the whole lane pauses until the reset time it states, and that stop doesn't count as a failed attempt. One gap: I track Claude cost only as launches against the budget, not as tokens.

cards.title: Self-scheduling hooks and the GPU keeper
questions: what is the gpu keeper agent

cards.answer: Two hooks add work on their own. The GPU keeper checks every hour whether the GPU lane is empty and, if so, queues one planning job to line up the next GPU work; it has done that 173 times. A periodic hook queues the hourly Overseer round and the six-hourly news fetch, but only from an allowlist of scripts and arguments, at most hourly, and only with an approval note. Editing the config cannot make it run an arbitrary command, which is the point of the allowlist.

cards.title: Why files instead of agent chat
questions: why don't the agents talk to each other in real time

what are the 539 handoff documents
what is the benefit of coordinating through files
cards.answer: Agents don't talk to each other in real time. They coordinate through files with owners: dependencies in the queue, dated handoff documents, a shared memory and a decision log. I chose this over agent-to-agent chat because every exchange then leaves a record that a new session, a reviewer or I can read later, and nothing depends on two agents being awake at once. A job can name the jobs it waits for, so one department's output becomes another's input without polling. There are 539 handoff documents across 11 departments, and they supersede by date, never by version number.

cards.title: The decision log and phone questions
questions: how many founder decisions are logged

what does a tap on the brief do
294 decisions since sep 30
cards.answer: My decisions go into an append-only log: 294 entries since Sep 30. Questions reach me as multiple choice with a recommended option, often on my phone from a morning brief page, and a tap appends a line. A later line for the same question supersedes the earlier one, so history is never rewritten. Agents search the log before asking me anything, and memory recall always shows my recorded decisions first.

cards.title: Shared memory rules enforced by tooling
questions: how many memory files do the agents share
what are one fact memory files

why is the memory body capped at 1200 characters
how are near duplicate memories refused
why does memory search run on the cpu
what embedding model does memory use

what rules does the memory tool enforce
cards.answer: There are 555 one-fact memory files across the departments. Each department writes only its own memories and reads everyone's. The tool enforces the rules a model won't reliably hold on its own: every memory names a source file that exists (its hash is stored), the body is capped at 1,200 characters, and near-duplicates are refused. Search runs on a small embedding model kept on the CPU, so recall still works while the GPU is busy.

cards.title: Memory sleep: nightly pruning
questions: what is memory sleep
what happens to memories every night
how are stale memories retired
what happens when a memory's source changed
what is the second pass of memory sleep
why is the memory judge switched off
what flags snapshots older than seven days
how do you stop memory from going stale
cards.answer: Every night a mechanical pass retires memories whose source is gone, hides ones whose source changed until an agent re-checks them, flags snapshots older than seven days, and flags duplicates. A second pass, where a local model checks memories against my decisions, is written but switched off until it passes its own evaluation. I won't let a model judge memories before I've measured how well it judges. The mechanical pass runs now; the judge pass is not live.

cards.title: Code ownership map and the scope guard
questions: how is code ownership enforced for the agents

what does the check mode do
why does the scope guard always exit 0
what does powershell do to non zero exit codes
why does a hook that blocks by exit code fail on windows
how does the scope guard deny a write

cards.answer: A machine-readable ownership map assigns every folder and code path to one of the 15 product agents: each department's own folder plus 62 owned code paths, with 5 paths reserved for me. A sync script writes each agent's scope from that map, and a check mode fails if any agent file drifts. The detail I'm glad I caught: on Windows, PowerShell collapses every non-zero exit to 1, which the agent runtime treats as a warning. So the scope guard always exits 0 and denies through an explicit "deny" decision in its output.

cards.title: Claude versus local models: the split
questions: why do some agents use claude and others local models
what runs on claude and what runs on the gpu

cards.answer: The split follows three things: usage (Claude is budgeted; the GPU is mine to fill), privacy (sensitive user data never goes to a cloud model, a rule rather than a preference) and fit (bulk work wants throughput, review wants judgment). Claude runs engineering, review, planning and research synthesis. Local open models do extraction, generation, grading, local agents and every draft of public text, where I approve each draft. Of the 754 Claude-lane jobs since Oct 2, 458 ran on Sonnet, 270 on Opus and 26 on Fable, chosen per job so a status check doesn't cost what a design review does.

cards.answer: Each department sits on a named local seat, mapped in one editable file, so no department is tied to a model in code. I picked seats by measuring on this card. Code is Qwen3 Coder 30B at temperature 0.15, which stayed fully on the GPU at a 32k context (about 30.5 GB). Prose is Qwen3 32B at 0.7 and is the only seat allowed to draft public text. Admin is the same base at 0.4. Alt-code is Devstral Small 2 24B, opt-in only, because it spilled about 18% to the CPU on the same task.

cards.title: The GPU lease: one big model at a time
questions: what is the gpu lease
why can't vllm and ollama share the gpu
how much of the gpu does vllm reserve
how much memory does a 32b qwen seat need on ollama
what happens when ollama collides with vllm

what are the three vllm profiles
what gpu does the workstation have
rtx 5090 with 32 gb setup

how is the gpu switch verified

cards.answer: The workstation has one RTX 5090 with 32 GB. A vLLM server reserves 94% of the card when it starts, and a 32B Qwen seat on Ollama needs about 20 GB, so they can't share. When they collide Ollama doesn't fail loudly: it spills to the CPU and runs about ten times slower. So the GPU is a lease with exactly one holder: idle, a vLLM server (an 8B generation model, Qwen3 32B AWQ, or Qwen3 VL 32B for vision and extraction), or the local Ollama seats. After every switch I check actual memory use and server health rather than assuming it worked.

cards.title: GPU switches never interrupt running work
questions: will a gpu switch interrupt a running job
what happens if a generation is live when a switch is requested

what are the gpu time windows
is the gpu scheduler live or a dry run
what runs overnight on the gpu

what does the restore script do
why not race a half written output file
cards.answer: A switch never interrupts running GPU work. If a generation, extraction or grading process is live, a switch away from it is refused and asked again on the next tick. Generation can resume, but a half-written output file isn't worth a race for the sake of a schedule. A separate restore script hands the card back to the vision model after a temporary switch, with the same refusal when work is running. I also wrote time windows (generation overnight, local agents in the daytime), but that scheduler is a dry run today: it logs what it would do.

cards.title: Review gates, CI and protected tests
questions: how do review gates work for the agents
who can block a merge or release

what is the pressure test of 84 probes

cards.answer: The quality agent can block a merge, release or content batch on quality, and the security agent can block one that weakens a control, each with a written reason; I can override either. The Principal Architect integrates changes and runs the ownership audit first. CI runs the product suite on Ubuntu and Windows, then proves that 14 protected tests actually ran and passed, because a deleted or skipped test leaves the build green and the guarantee gone. An 84-probe pressure test follows. Findings are one of four kinds: safety or evidence blocker, integration blocker, publication-only blocker, or later improvement. Nicer writing is never a blocker.

cards.answer: On Oct 19 the product suite ran 1,499 tests on my working checkout: 1,496 passed and 3 failed, all three in one module that is mid-change. Those three are open, not hidden. The job queue has its own tests for the periodic hook (10, passing), and Agent City has its own suite, which ran 340 tests that day with one error still open. I'd rather report the open failures plainly than quote a clean number I haven't earned.

cards.title: Authority levels: what needs me
questions: what are the authority levels
which decisions need the founder
what can agents decide without asking
what does a department head approve
what is a level 3 decision
what is the release boundary
does any agent publish or push
why does the shell guard deny git push
who authorises a full generation run
how did you stop agents asking about everything

cards.answer: On Oct 18 I wrote down which decisions actually need me, so agents stop asking about things they can safely decide. Level 1: agents act without asking on isolated bugs, tests, formatting, wording that keeps its meaning, approved requirements and changes that pass the checks. Level 2: a department head approves changes to internal checks and bounded technical changes within policy. Level 3 comes only to me: the evidence standard, product promises, sensitive data, significant spending, release scope, public deployment and a full generation run. No agent publishes; the shell guard denies every git push.

cards.title: Agent City as a deterministic projection
questions: how does agent city decide an agent's state
what is the state precedence in agent city
what does offline mean versus sleeping in agent city
how does agent city poll
why polling instead of server push
what does run now do in agent city
can run now bypass a usage pause

what is the idempotency key window
what is the done log
how many finished jobs are in the done log

cards.answer: Agent City is a read-mostly projection: it owns no scheduling and runs no work. One pure function turns a few authoritative fields into one state with fixed precedence: blocked, waiting on me, working, queued, offline, paused, scheduled soon, sleeping, idle. Unreachable means offline, never asleep. Browsers poll every 5 seconds with a cursor; I chose polling over push for simplicity. Run now sets aside one date gate and never overrides approvals, dependencies, a usage pause or the budget. Commands are previewable, and the same key within 24 hours returns the stored result. The Done log holds 1,060 finished jobs, and the town is reachable only over my private network.

cards.title: Known limits and what I would change
questions: what would you do differently in the agent architecture
what are the known limits of the agent system
why is parsing text for usage limits fragile

why would you use sqlite instead of json files
what are per job work contracts
are work contracts built

what would a sandbox change
which parts are only partly built
why is the foreman paused
what is not measured in the agent system
cards.answer: Five things. The queue detects a Claude usage limit by reading output, and on Oct 9 an agent's report mentioned the limit and paused the lane for a day; I anchored the pattern, but the real fix is a structured exit signal. Shell writes are guarded by heuristics, so I'd rather run each agent in a sandbox where out-of-scope paths aren't writable. Per-job work contracts (allowed paths, tools, done criteria, budget) are planned, not built. The queue keeps 1,129 jobs in one JSON file, and I'd use SQLite from day one. The foreman is paused and the memory judge is off.
